name: Framework Computer Inc.
origin_detail: Founded in San Francisco in January 2020 by Nirav Patel (founder and CEO) to sell repairable, upgradeable laptops; first Framework Laptop (13) fulfilled July 2021.
openness_notes: Hardware column. At launch (2021) only peripheral interfaces were open to developers via the Expansion Card Developer Program (level 1; exact release date of the reference designs not verified). In January 2022 Framework open-sourced its embedded-controller firmware (BSD-3-Clause, based on Chrome EC) and in April 2022 published mainboard documentation and CAD. Today its GitHub repositories carry chassis CAD (STEP) under CC BY 4.0, 2D drawings, connector pinouts, partial schematics, expansion card, expansion bay and input-module reference designs, and EC firmware for all models; the UEFI firmware (InsydeH2O) remains proprietary and full mainboard schematics and PCB layouts are not published. Open firmware plus open module interfaces with closed core boards = level 2.

risk_events: 2021-2022: early AMD shipments delayed by electrical and firmware issues
2024: Ars Technica reported Framework had fallen short on timely BIOS and firmware updates (company acknowledged; progress noted June 2025)
2025-10: controversy over sponsoring politically polarising software projects
2026: Laptop 13 Pro shipping slipped from late June to late July over manufacturing issues

2026-08: notified all customers that names, email and postal addresses and phone numbers were exposed through a zero-day attack on its business-intelligence provider Metabase; payment data not included
2026-11: memory and storage price increases after using up earlier, lower-cost DDR5 inventory
robustness: Relies on contract manufacturing and closed UEFI firmware from Insyde, so long-term support depends on the company, but published CAD, pinouts and the open EC firmware let owners and third parties repair, reuse and extend hardware independently. Small VC base (about $45M disclosed) for a multi-product hardware maker.
physical_science_relevance: Repairable, documented mainboards can be reused as embedded lab computers (Framework publishes printable cases for bare mainboards); open EC firmware and Linux-first support (Laptop 13 Pro shipped Ubuntu-first in 2026) suit research users.
openness_effect_assessment: Framework uses openness of interfaces and documentation (CC BY 4.0 CAD, open EC firmware, expansion-card reference designs) as a product feature for repairability and a third-party module ecosystem, while keeping core board designs and BIOS closed. It has grown from one laptop to four product lines in five years on modest funding (about $45M disclosed), but openness has not removed the firmware-maintenance burden that drew its main criticism in 2024.
key_takeaway: Framework is a US example of partial, interface-level openness as a business strategy: publish the module interfaces, CAD and EC firmware so customers and third parties can repair and extend the machine, but keep the mainboard design and BIOS proprietary. It sits at level 2 and shows that 'open where it builds an ecosystem, closed where it protects the core' can sustain a VC-backed hardware startup through 2026, with firmware update cadence as the main weakness.
